companies.desc: The provincial-level office set up to run this World Bank loan for the Sichuan provincial government, with a project management office and implementation unit in each of the eight project towns. The completion report records no activity for it outside Bank-financed work.

sichuan-small-towns-unfinished-resettlem.community: The project widened and rebuilt roads, water and sewerage networks, canals and river embankments in eight towns in Sichuan. The completion report gives the outcome: land acquisition took 2,387.32 mu of collective land and 526.95 mu of state-owned land, affecting 2,802 households or 8,720 people; houses measuring 142,192.3 were demolished, affecting 605 households against 528 households estimated in the resettlement plans - the report's text gives that figure in cubic metres and its own table in square metres; and structures measuring 39,867.25 belonging to 34 enterprises or other entities were demolished. Separately, works added in Liujiang Town in 2015 took 19.7 mu of land from 19 households, 83 people, in Yang Village and Lianghe Village. The report then records what had not happened. By the time the loan closed on 31 December 2016, 348 households in four counties and districts had still not been resettled: 148 in Xinjin, 54 in Miyi, 80 in Zizhong and 66 in Jialing. The report gives the reason: the resettlement houses for this project were only a small part of large resettlement sites that local governments were building for displaced people from this and other domestic projects, construction of those sites was delayed, and their implementation was not under the control of the Bank's project. A supplementary resettlement plan was agreed between Sichuan and the Bank, with commitment letters from local governments and willingness letters from households, under which most of the remaining households were to be allocated houses by March 2017 and to get their keys by September 2017. By the completion mission at the end of March 2017, three months after the loan closed, 114 households in Zizhong and Jialing had still not been resettled. The report records that the completion mission was informed that households in those two counties changed their minds and did not take the county government's offer of an existing resettlement site, deciding to wait for the originally planned housing, which is closer to where they had lived, while continuing to draw monthly transition subsidies of 240 yuan a person in Zizhong; 25 households in Jialing District had signed a willingness letter in December 2016 to wait until the end of 2018. The report's own schedule shows 38 households in Jialing not due to be resettled until December 2018 and 58 households in Zizhong not until June 2018, two years after the loan closed. The report also states that compensation was paid in compliance with Chinese regulations and Bank policy, that in some cases extra government budget was provided to raise compensation to replacement cost at the time of implementation rather than the standard set in the plan years earlier, that external monitoring found the income of affected residents higher than before the project, and that no complaints were received throughout the project.
sichuan-small-towns-unfinished-resettlem.displaced_label: households whose houses were demolished, against 528 estimated in the resettlement plans; 2,802 households or 8,720 people were affected by land acquisition (World Bank completion report)
sichuan-small-towns-unfinished-resettlem.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 6,119 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's own completion report counts 2,802 households or 8,720 people affected by land acquisition and 605 households whose houses were demolished. No figure matching 6,119 appears in the completion report, in the Independent Evaluation Group's review or in the appraisal document, and the documents do not explain the gap. ICIJ’s own method page states what its figures count. It looked for what the Bank’s documents call "Project-Affected People (PAP)" or "displaced people", searching those documents for the words "affected", "PAP" or "displaced". Where a document counted only households, it says it was necessary to look up the average number of family members per household. Because the documents do not all separate temporary impacts from permanent ones, it "decided to include all impacts", and it says the impact counted "can be as modest as losing less than 1 percent of their land or income". It drew mainly on resettlement action plans, which are written before the work is done, and looked to completion reports where no resettlement document existed. Its data stops at 31 December 2014.
sichuan-small-towns-unfinished-resettlem.outcome: The loan closed on 31 December 2016 with 348 households not yet resettled, and 114 of them were still not resettled three months later. The Independent Evaluation Group rated the risk that the remaining resettlement would be further delayed or not completed as Substantial. For what happened after that, the review has no document: it states that the project team told it by email on 29 October 2017 that as of September 2017 agreements had been signed for house distribution in Xinjin and Miyi, that houses for 14 households in Jialing were to be completed by October 2017 and for 4 more by December 2017, that houses for 38 households in Jialing were to be delivered by December 2018, and that construction for 58 households in Zizhong was to start in October 2017 with houses ready by June 2018. The Bank's filing for the project ends with that review and a 2017 audit report, and neither records whether those dates were met.

sichuan-small-towns-unfinished-resettlem.confidence_note: The household counts, the county breakdown and the dates all come from the Bank's own completion report and from the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report. The lender is reporting on its own project. No independent press report, non-governmental field study, court record or Inspection Panel complaint about this resettlement was found. Searches in English and in Chinese returned only World Bank documents. The completion report attributes part of the delay to the households' own choice to wait for the originally planned housing while drawing monthly subsidies, and it states that compensation was paid in compliance with Bank policy, that incomes rose and that no complaints were received. It does not say how long any household went without permanent housing or how many people the 348 households held; it gives the transition subsidy only for Zizhong, at 240 yuan a person a month. The post-closing position rests on an email from the Bank project team to the evaluators, not on a document. The completion report gives the demolished housing figure in cubic metres in its text and in square metres in its own table. Its data sheet gives the report's date as 14 April 2017 while its cover page gives 31 May 2017. The Independent Evaluation Group's review carries no date on the document itself; the date given is the one in the Bank's own document-system record for it.
sichuan-small-towns-unfinished-resettlem.conditions: The loan was environmental category B and triggered the Bank's policies on environmental assessment, physical cultural resources and involuntary resettlement. Individual resettlement action plans were prepared for each sub-component with a summary plan covering all of them, disclosed locally in Chinese between 2 and 17 July 2010 and at the Bank's InfoShop on 7 July 2010; a further plan for works added in Liujiang Town was disclosed locally on 30 July 2015 and at the InfoShop on 29 July 2015. An independent external resettlement monitoring agent reported alongside the project office's own monitoring, and the loan paid for that monitoring under its capacity-building component. When resettlement was left unfinished at closing, a supplementary resettlement action plan was agreed between Sichuan and the Bank, with signed commitment letters from local governments and willingness letters from households, and external monitoring was contracted to continue until the resettlement was complete (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 31 May 2017).

qufu-gupan-pond-demolition.community: Two years into implementation, 588 houses in a 13-hectare area around the Gupan Pond in the Ming Old City of Qufu were demolished in 44 days, except for five buildings designated as historic. The completion report states that neither China's State Administration of Cultural Heritage, nor the World Bank, nor UNESCO was informed about the planned demolition. The site sits inside the buffer zone of the Temple and Cemetery of Confucius and the Kong Family Mansion World Heritage Site. The completion report records the clearance as one major incident of non-compliance with the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy, and its lessons section says the non-compliance was found when the local implementation unit moved ahead with resettling residents at the Gupan Pond without an approved resettlement plan. The subproject was also out of compliance with UNESCO's buffer-zone requirements for World Heritage sites and was cancelled at the restructuring of April 2016, although the Bank kept the resettlement linked to the project. UNESCO's World Heritage Centre wrote to China on 9 December 2013 about the razing of the housing; China replied on 28 March 2014, describing the work as a comprehensive renovation project partly funded by the World Bank, covering 13.34 hectares of the buffer zone, and stating that 588 households had been moved since the first half of 2013. The World Heritage Committee's decision 38 COM 7B.11 of 2014 noted the redevelopment and expressed concern about its potential impact on the site's Outstanding Universal Value, including its authenticity and integrity. An ICOMOS reactive monitoring mission visited from 9 to 12 December 2014. The next state-of-conservation report, considered in 2016 under decision 40 COM 7B.32, records that the 13.34-hectare area had held 588 households, that most of the housing had been built after the 1970s and about a third of it was dilapidated, that five buildings were found historically valuable and saved, and that no construction had followed the demolition, and that the suspension of the reconstruction project had a negative impact on the public credibility of the local government. Across the whole project the completion report counts 790 households resettled - 588 in Qufu and 202 in Zoucheng - affecting 3,612 people. The resettlement plans had estimated demolition of urban housing belonging to 346 households, 1,211 people, in Qufu and 342 households, 1,198 people, in Zoucheng. In Qufu 86,300 square metres of urban housing was demolished against 40,524 planned, and 206.5 mu of state-owned land was permanently occupied against 94.3 mu planned. In Zoucheng 33,274.86 square metres of urban housing and 2,051.88 square metres of rural housing were demolished, affecting 190 households, 760 people, and 12 households, 52 people. Across both cities 204 shops were demolished, affecting 1,014 people. Unlicensed buildings were also taken: 194 households, 692 people, in Qufu and 78 households, 213 people, in Zoucheng. Resettlement cost 492.63 million yuan in Qufu and 178.83 million yuan in Zoucheng. The completion report also says that at the start of implementation project activities were largely decided without sufficient consultation with local communities, and that a social development team was later commissioned on the Bank team's recommendation to run public consultation. On the Gupan Pond site itself the report says the Bank task team took on the management of the resettlement after the subproject was dropped, that all affected households received resettlement houses before the loan closed, that the resettlement compound was about 500 metres from the original houses, that families moving there came from the same neighbourhood and kept their community ties, that the new housing had solar panels, heating, parking and storage, and that house values in the area rose from about 3,000 to 5,600 yuan a square metre after the resettlement began.

The Independent Evaluation Group recorded no reason for disagreement on any rating.

qufu-gupan-pond-demolition.confidence_note: The demolition is recorded outside the Bank. UNESCO's World Heritage Centre raised it with China in December 2013, the World Heritage Committee addressed it in two decisions, and an ICOMOS reactive monitoring mission visited the site in December 2014. That is why this is not rated as resting on the lender alone. Two limits on the independent record: the figure of 588 households moved is China's own statement to UNESCO, not a finding by UNESCO; and UNESCO's concern is about the World Heritage site, not about the people who were moved. On the people, the Bank's completion report is the only source. It is the lender reporting on its own project, and it contains both the non-compliance finding and a favourable account of the destination housing, the distance moved and the rise in local house prices. No independent press report, field study or court record about the households themselves was found; searches in English and in Chinese returned only World Bank and UNESCO documents. The completion report's own figures do not fully line up: its summary says 588 households were resettled in Qufu, while its lessons section refers to 251 households having originally lived at the Gupan Pond, and no document explains the difference. The Independent Evaluation Group's review carries no date on the document itself; the date given is the one in the Bank's own document-system record for it.
qufu-gupan-pond-demolition.conditions: The loan was environmental category B and triggered the Bank's policies on environmental assessment, physical cultural resources and involuntary resettlement. A resettlement action plan was prepared before approval and disclosed locally and at the Bank's InfoShop in November 2010; an abbreviated plan for activities added at restructuring was disclosed locally in July 2015 and at the InfoShop in December 2015. An external monitoring team reported on compliance with the involuntary resettlement policy twice a year, and a further contract for external monitoring of resettlement in Qufu was added to the project at restructuring. The Gupan Pond clearance went ahead before a resettlement plan for it had been approved, which the completion report records as a major incident of non-compliance with that policy; the site also fell under UNESCO's buffer-zone requirements for World Heritage sites, which the completion report says the demolition did not meet. After the subcomponent was cancelled the Bank kept the resettlement linked to the project and the Bank task team took over its management, communicating directly with UNESCO and the State Administration of Cultural Heritage on a revised urban design (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 19 December 2017).

xiangyang-panggong-resettlement-housing-.community: The project built about 20 kilometres of primary and secondary roads in the Panggong area of Xiangcheng District, which the completion report describes as formerly a rural area with rural roads and streets, together with a bus corridor and terminal on Route 13 and traffic management works. The completion report gives the outcome of the land acquisition: at project closing all 776 families affected by land acquisition had been compensated and 768 families had been resettled. The number of people to be resettled rose above the original estimate because the city's master plan changed and because households that had been surveyed voluntarily split into more households. The report records what went wrong. The mid-term review of May 2015 named resettlement as the critical issue. Funds for land acquisition were secured, but funds were not available for the resettlement housing; despite an agreement at the mid-term review to meet targets by October 2015, work on the resettlement housing started only in 2016 and some of it was finished only in 2017. Because the housing was late, construction of some of the roads in Panggong was delayed by more than two years, and the project's closing date had to be extended twice, from September 2017 to July 2019. The report names the cause as a lack of coordination between three bodies: the project management office, responsible for road construction; the Xiangcheng District Government, responsible for land acquisition; and the Xiangcheng Urban Investment Company, responsible for building the resettlement housing. All three were committed to the work, the report says, but their plans and priorities were not coordinated in time. The municipal government changed the compensation process in 2015 and introduced cash compensation as an alternative in order to speed matters up, and the Bank's social specialist made a separate support mission in December 2017 to deal with resettlement issues. The report also records the other side. It says resettlement was an opportunity for some families to improve their housing significantly, that housing visited by the completion mission appeared to be of satisfactory quality, that the residents met expressed satisfaction with their new homes, and that no resettlement-related complaints were received during the project. Household surveys by the social safeguard monitoring consultant found the average annual income of the sampled affected households rose from RMB 28,000 in 2012 to RMB 44,000 in 2018, an annual rate of 11.5 per cent, which the report says is more than the growth of Xiangyang's gross domestic product, and that the value of the assets those households owned after resettlement, mainly housing, was about four to five times what it had been before. The report adds that unfavourable customary practices for women on resettlement existed in the project area, so that without the project women might not have had access to information or the same level of compensation as men, and that women made up half the participants in the local resettlement meetings.

nanning-urban-environment-resettlement.community: The project built six wastewater treatment plants and rehabilitated three rivers in Nanning. The completion report compares plan with outcome: 1,577 households, 7,130 people, were planned to be affected and 1,904 households, 7,968 people, actually were; permanent and temporary land acquisition planned at 2,175.19 and 733.1 mu came to 2,687.073 mu; and 4,428.86 square metres of houses and 89,696.84 square metres of other structures were demolished against 34,871 square metres of structures planned. The report records two things left unfinished. First, four village groups in Nanxiang Village - Nos. 1, 2, 9 and 11 - had not received the official certificate for the commercial land they had been granted; their land acquisition and compensation agreements were signed with the resettlement office of the Jiangnan District Government. Group No. 1 got its certificate by December 2016; Groups Nos. 2 and 9 were expected to receive theirs by December 2017 and Group No. 11 by December 2018, two and a half years after the loan closed. The report says the certificates were delayed because the documents the groups submitted were incomplete, and says elsewhere that all the compensation is completed and that the issuance of the remaining certificates is a matter of time because the necessary documents have since been submitted by the village groups. The project office agreed in an official letter of 10 April 2017 to keep working with the Jiangnan District Government on the issue and to report to the Bank every six months until the certificates were issued. The last two implementation status reports and aide memoires had recorded incomplete compensation of commercial land for Village Group No. 11; the completion report says that in March 2017 the Bank team, after reviewing the land acquisition and compensation agreements signed between the village group and the resettlement office of the Jiangnan District Government, found the group had already been fully compensated with its entitled 13.22 mu of commercial land, and that the project office confirmed this by email on 19 and 21 March 2017. Second, 10 households in the residential area of Tianyu were to have been resettled by the end of 2016; after the project closed they decided to take full monetary compensation and build new houses in the village instead of moving to apartments in Tianyu Huayuan, and the report says all 10 were fully compensated by December 2016. The Independent Evaluation Group's review adds that land acquisition and resettlement for the whole wastewater component was complete by the end of June 2013, but that delays occurred under the river rehabilitation component, particularly over land reallocation for Nanxiang Village and the construction of the resettlement site in Wuxiang New District, and that those delays were part of the reason a section of the river rehabilitation component was cancelled. The completion report states that all compensation required for the project was provided, that affected people experienced no significant adverse impacts, that resettled people meeting the landless-farmer criteria were entitled to pensions, unemployment allowances and job training, and that completion and monitoring surveys confirmed livelihoods were restored and compensation paid in full. The Zhuang people are a majority of the population in the project areas. A social assessment at preparation concluded they were mostly economically integrated and culturally assimilated and so unlikely to be adversely affected, and consultation before implementation found them supportive, so no indigenous peoples' plan was prepared, although the Bank's policy on indigenous peoples had been triggered.
nanning-urban-environment-resettlement.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 7,191 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's own completion report counts 1,904 households, 7,968 people, actually affected against 1,577 households, 7,130 people, planned, and 4,428.86 square metres of houses demolished. It does not separate people relocated from people affected in other ways, so no count of people moved is given here. No figure matching 7,191 appears in the completion report, in the Independent Evaluation Group's review or in the appraisal document, and the documents do not explain the gap. ICIJ’s own method page states what its figures count. It looked for what the Bank’s documents call "Project-Affected People (PAP)" or "displaced people", searching those documents for the words "affected", "PAP" or "displaced". Where a document counted only households, it says it was necessary to look up the average number of family members per household. Because the documents do not all separate temporary impacts from permanent ones, it "decided to include all impacts", and it says the impact counted "can be as modest as losing less than 1 percent of their land or income". It drew mainly on resettlement action plans, which are written before the work is done, and looked to completion reports where no resettlement document existed. Its data stops at 31 December 2014.
nanning-urban-environment-resettlement.outcome: The loan closed on 30 June 2016 with land certificates owed to three village groups in Jiangnan District, the last of them not expected until December 2018, and with the project office committed to reporting to the Bank every six months until they were issued. The Bank's filing for the project ends with the review of September 2017 and a financial audit report, and neither records whether the certificates were delivered. Separately, the Bank's Integrity Vice Presidency investigated this project alongside two others in China and found that a company it does not name misrepresented the availability of its key personnel in the technical proposals it submitted under this project; the Bank imposed debarment with conditional release on that company and a second company, which the report says share a parent company, and the sanction extends to any entity either of them directly or indirectly controls. The company names are redacted from the public report. The completion report also records that a consulting contract was held up for more than 14 months because of the firm's possible connection with a debarred firm, and was then terminated.

liaoning-coastal-zone-resettlement.community: The project rebuilt urban roads, water and wastewater works and drainage in six cities and counties of coastal and western Liaoning. The completion report gives the outcome of the land acquisition in one sentence: 760.6 mu of land was taken, affecting 1,843 people in 492 households, and the total number of households physically resettled was 548. A resettlement office was set up under each city's project implementation unit, and a consulting firm that is a subsidiary of the Liaoning Social Academy monitored compliance from outside the project. Each implementation unit ran a grievance mechanism; according to the completion mission's interviews, when a unit received questions or concerns from affected people it answered by telephone or a visit to the site, and no formal appeal was raised under the project. At appraisal the Bank rated as moderate the risk to social and environmental safeguards arising from the cities' limited ability to compensate affected people in a timely way. The Independent Evaluation Group's review states that the 548 households received appropriate compensation in a timely manner, and attributes that not to a document but to the Bank task team's email to the evaluators of 3 June 2020. The review also reports the land taken as 760 cubic metres, where the completion report gives 760.6 mu, a unit of area. When loan savings were used in 2018 to add road rehabilitation in Kuandian, no resettlement plan was required because the land had been acquired years earlier; a public consultation report was prepared for new road works in Lingyuan, recording interviews with women, disabled people and elderly people. Several participating city governments could not produce their share of the funding on time, which the completion report names as a cause of delay across the project, and in Panjin the counterpart funding requirement was cut from 30 to 10 per cent, which the report says relieved the city's finances and allowed more local money to go to resettlement and the project.

han-river-urban-environment-resettlement.community: The project built wastewater collection and treatment and solid waste facilities in second-tier cities along the Han River in Hubei. The appraisal document of 24 March 2008 planned to relocate 206 rural households and said more than 5,600 people would be affected by land acquisition and relocation across nine cities and counties, with 1,908.57 mu of rural land acquired and 37,764.63 square metres of housing demolished. Its table counts 4,649 people affected by land acquisition only, 691 to be relocated, 231 affected by both land acquisition and house demolition, and 335 attached to non-residential units. The outcome is in the borrower's section of the completion report: 1,432.53 mu, 95.5 hectares, was acquired and 671 households were affected, mostly from the Hanchuan landfill subproject; 14,446.09 square metres of housing was demolished, affecting 83 households, mostly from the Shayang landfill subproject. More than 70 and 80 per cent of the 88 households surveyed said they supported the project and were satisfied with the compensation for land acquisition and housing demolition. In Shayang, which the Bank's own section calls a best-practice resettlement programme, only six households took cash compensation and 72 families chose to move into newly built apartments with vegetable plots, animal pens, a health clinic, a small supermarket and sports facilities. In Hanchuan a site that a consulting team had identified as waste land turned out to be occupied by fishing ponds, which the report says raised compensation costs considerably. In Xiaochang the households to be resettled were consulted on the options open to them. Displaced families were invited to take part in monitoring the construction of the resettlement sites, and the report says most complaints were dealt with and resolved satisfactorily. The borrower's section also records that air, groundwater and noise quality met the applicable standards at most of the subprojects, but that odour and groundwater around some old dump sites exceeded the limits, and that the regulators were to require the implementing agencies to make further improvements and install monitoring wells.

The completion report gives the outcome city by city. Permanent land acquisition came to 1,331.3 mu against 1,214 planned for the six cities that stayed in the project; temporary land occupation to 1,620.9 mu against 1,901.9; house demolition to 94,750.8 square metres against 131,799; and enterprise, institution and shop space affected to 16,090.8 square metres against 10,387.7. The number of affected people came to 4,220 against 4,718 planned for those six cities. Zaozhuang carried most of it: 753.4 mu of land, 77,056.7 square metres of housing and 3,548 affected people, with compensation of 238.24 million yuan. Surveys among the affected people indicated their living quality was better than before and their income had been restored or improved. Of all the affected population, 23 people in nine households in the Zaozhuang and Heze components were classified as vulnerable; the local government guaranteed their living standards would not be adversely affected and training and employment information were provided to their family members. The Independent Evaluation Group's review adds that resettlement went satisfactorily except in Qixia and Zaozhuang counties, because of the slow pace of land acquisition and resettlement, and that two project cities finished implementation only in 2013 largely for that reason.

shanghai-urban-environment-apl2-resettle.community: The project built sewers, water treatment and solid waste facilities in Shanghai. The resettlement plans at appraisal identified 1,112 project-affected people in 282 households, with 697.65 mu, 46 hectares, of compulsory land acquisition and 60 commercial enterprises to be affected or relocated. The completion report gives the outcome: 598.5 mu, 40 hectares, was actually acquired; 174 people in 44 households were affected; and 10 commercial enterprises were affected or relocated. Most of the reduction came from a change in construction method on the Western Trunk Sewer, where pipe-jacking replaced open-trench work in heavily built-up downtown areas, so that component moved nobody at all against a plan of 1,064 people in 266 households. The five subprojects financed through the district facility ran the other way: they moved 174 people in 44 households against a plan of 48 people in 16 households, and took 587 mu of land against 442 planned. Compensation for land acquisition, demolition of structures and resettlement came to RMB 188.26 million against RMB 448 million estimated at appraisal. Independent monitoring confirmed that the full compensation set out in each resettlement plan was paid; the final external monitoring report found all resettlement had followed the plans with no outstanding issues. Post-construction surveys by the independent monitoring consultant of every subproject where resettlement occurred found no instance of a negative impact on the area around the affected people, that compensation was paid in every case for land acquisition and resettlement, and that rural households were paid for losses on farming and crop plantings. Rural affected people were offered retraining through local village committees to make a living by other means, and the report says those who took it were very satisfied with the improvement in their living standards and household income. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 16 March 2017 lowered the outcome to Satisfactory, finding no evidence to demonstrate the increased efficiency of the wastewater treatment process, and raised the risk to the development outcome to Modest, because the raw water intake for the Nanjing-Longtan water treatment plant was only 1.2 km downstream of a small-river oil wharf; its table prints the completion report's risk rating as Negligible, which is not the word the report uses (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 7 June 2016; IEG ICR Review, 16 March 2017).

jiangsu-water-wastewater-resettlement.community: The project expanded water supply in Danyang, Taixing, Yancheng and Zhenjiang and wastewater collection and treatment in Danyang, Nanjing and Taixing. Eleven volumes of resettlement action plans were prepared and disclosed in 2008 and later. The appraisal document of 16 April 2009 set out what was expected: 34 hectares of land to be permanently acquired, including 25 hectares of collective land from which 1,053 people derived part of their income; 350 hectares to be temporarily occupied, including 145 hectares of collective land from which 3,433 people derived part of their income; 117 households with 417 people to have their houses demolished, 104 of those households and 355 of those people in Nanjing; and 10 enterprises and 80 shops to be affected. The completion report gives the outcome in a single sentence: 494 project-affected people were properly resettled and/or compensated, 59 hectares of land was acquired and 1,043 hectares was temporarily occupied during construction. Many of the affected people started their own livelihood restoration measures, such as job training. The report says reducing potential resettlement was a key criterion when alternatives were analysed at preparation, that project-affected people were engaged through public participation and mobilisation meetings to collect their comments and opinions, that the grievance and appeals mechanisms were well publicised, that the implementation units restored public facilities to high standards after temporary land occupation, and that land acquisition and resettlement generally proceeded smoothly, with compliance rated satisfactory. One sub-component was cancelled over resettlement: the Danyang wastewater works in Shicheng urban district, for lack of progress with land acquisition and resettlement on a linked river rehabilitation project.
jiangsu-water-wastewater-resettlement.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 6,388 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's own completion report counts 494 project-affected people 'properly resettled and/or compensated' - a phrase that does not separate those who were moved from those who were only paid - and 59 hectares of land acquired. The appraisal document had planned for 117 households with 417 people to have their houses demolished and for 1,053 people to lose part of their income to permanent land acquisition. Because no document gives a count of people actually relocated, no such figure is given here. No figure matching 6,388 appears in the completion report, in the Independent Evaluation Group's review or in the appraisal document, and the documents do not explain the gap. ICIJ’s own method page states what its figures count. It looked for what the Bank’s documents call "Project-Affected People (PAP)" or "displaced people", searching those documents for the words "affected", "PAP" or "displaced". Where a document counted only households, it says it was necessary to look up the average number of family members per household. Because the documents do not all separate temporary impacts from permanent ones, it "decided to include all impacts", and it says the impact counted "can be as modest as losing less than 1 percent of their land or income". It drew mainly on resettlement action plans, which are written before the work is done, and looked to completion reports where no resettlement document existed. Its data stops at 31 December 2014.
jiangsu-water-wastewater-resettlement.outcome: The loan closed on 31 December 2015 a year late, with the completion report rating the project Highly Satisfactory and recording that land acquisition and resettlement proceeded smoothly and that compliance with social safeguards was satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 16 March 2017 lowered the outcome rating to Satisfactory, finding no evidence of the claimed increase in wastewater treatment efficiency, and raised the risk to the development outcome because the raw water intake for the Nanjing-Longtan water treatment plant sits only 1.2 km downstream of an oil wharf. The review adds no resettlement finding of its own and repeats the completion report's single sentence.

jiangsu-water-wastewater-resettlement.confidence_note: This is the thinnest of the batch on the outcome. The whole of the completion report's resettlement outcome is one sentence, and its key verb is 'resettled and/or compensated', which leaves it unknown how many of the 494 people lost a home and how many only lost land or income. The documented harm is therefore the land taken - 59 hectares permanently and 1,043 hectares temporarily - plus the appraisal plan for demolishing the houses of 117 households. Every figure comes from the Bank's own appraisal document, its completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report; the lender is reporting on its own project. No independent press report, non-governmental field study, court record or Inspection Panel complaint about this resettlement was found. Searches in English and in Chinese returned only World Bank documents. The report records the resettlement as having proceeded smoothly with satisfactory compliance. No village is named, no compensation rate is given, and neither document says what happened to the people on the cancelled Danyang sub-component or on the linked river rehabilitation project whose stalled resettlement caused the cancellation.
jiangsu-water-wastewater-resettlement.conditions: The loan was environmental category B and triggered the Bank's policy on involuntary resettlement. A resettlement policy framework and resettlement action plans were prepared, eleven volumes in all, covering the individual city components and including the resettlement issues of activities linked to the project but not financed by it; they were disclosed from August 2008, with a further plan for the Taixing regional water supply works disclosed in December 2010. The plans applied Chinese property and land law, Jiangsu's own land acquisition rules and the Bank's resettlement policy together. Rural houses were to be paid for at building replacement cost and urban houses, enterprises and shops at commercially valued price, with movement subsidies and transition allowances on top of compensation for assets, and compensation of construction materials for illegal structures. Farmers losing land were offered a choice between a larger single cash payment with free job training and a package of cash compensation with living subsidies and a pension plus free job training. Land acquisition and resettlement were monitored by an independent external agency which reported periodically, with key findings summarised in the half-yearly progress reports (Project Appraisal Document, 16 April 2009; Implementation Completion and Results Report, 7 June 2016).
jiangsu-water-wastewater-resettlement.drop_reason: Neither limb of the forward rule is met. The completion report's entire resettlement outcome is one sentence (paragraph 35, read in full): 494 project-affected people were 'properly resettled and/or compensated', 59 ha of land acquired and 1,043 ha temporarily occupied. The phrase does not say how many of the 494 were moved, so there is no document count of people or households relocated (limb a). What is left is land area with no identified people, no named village or site, no compensation rate, no household count for any demolition - the completion report records no housing demolition outcome at all - and no recorded failure: the report rates the project Highly Satisfactory and says land acquisition and resettlement proceeded smoothly with satisfactory compliance. The appraisal plan for demolishing the houses of 117 households is a plan, not harm. That is a count of people 'affected' with land area attached, which the forward rule cuts.
